passage:
“Why are you glaring at a spreadsheet?” Didi asked, leaning on Leela's door.
“I'm adding. School, seven hours, five days: thirty-five. Three coaching batches: twelve. Bus rides: eight. Homework: seven.”
“And sleep?”
“It's not on the sheet.” Leela's voice cracked. “Didi, it's sixty-two hours. Sixty-two, and I still fall behind. I keep telling myself I'm just not trying hard enough.”
Didi sat on the bed and took the pencil. “Sixty-two hours a week, before eating and before any rest. Who could try hard enough for that?”
“So it's not me?”
“It's the total. You're carrying a full-time job and calling yourself lazy.”
Leela laughed shakily and wiped her eyes. “Then what do I change?”
“Tomorrow we look at what each batch actually gives you.”

qa.q: How many hours a week did Leela's tally come to?
What was Leela feeling about herself before adding it up?
qa.a: Guilt and self-doubt: she kept telling herself she was not trying hard enough.

qa.q: What could Leela do next with the total, and why?
qa.a: She could compare what each batch adds and trim or move the least useful one, because the problem is the total load, not her effort.

qa.q: How does Didi see Leela's problem?
qa.a: Didi sees a younger sister blaming herself for a timetable that would exhaust anyone, and wants her to see the load as the real problem.

grounding: A student adds up school, coaching, travel and homework, and sees that the problem is total load, not lack of effort.

passage:
In Class 11, I was sure my problem was laziness. I'm Tanuja, and I was always behind, always tired, and always telling myself to try harder.

One Sunday my friend Arnab said, "Just add up your week. Actually add it."

So I did, on the back of a physics notebook. School: 36 hours. Three coaching batches: 12 hours. Travel between them on two buses: 7 hours. Homework and coaching assignments: 7 hours. Total: 62 hours. Rest: I searched for it and couldn't find any. Even Sunday mornings had a test series.

I looked at that number for a long time. Sixty-two. A full-time job is less.

It changed how I saw myself. I wasn't lazy. I was overloaded. The question wasn't how to push harder. It was what to cut.

I took the sheet to my parents that evening. That was the start of dropping one batch.

qa.q: How did Tanuja feel after seeing the number?
qa.a: Tanuja felt stunned, then relieved, realising the problem was overload rather than laziness.

qa.q: What else could Tanuja add to the audit before talking to the parents?
qa.a: Tanuja could mark which batches actually help most, so the conversation is about what to cut, not only how tired Tanuja is.

qa.q: How might Tanuja's parents see the sheet?
qa.a: They may be surprised by the total and more willing to talk about cutting a batch, since the numbers make the load clear.

grounding: A reflective account of a Class 11 student adding up school, three coaching batches, travel and homework, finding 62 hours and no rest, and seeing the problem as total load.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Class 11 Science

Hansa came to me because she felt she was "not working hard enough". Her friend Lalremsiami had brought her, saying she cried in the washroom after a test.

Rather than talk about effort, I asked Hansa to list every fixed hour in her week. She wrote: school, 35; coaching, three batches, 13; buses and autos, 8; homework, 6. She added it herself: 62. I asked where rest was. She looked at the sheet for a while and said, "There isn't any."

She was quiet, then said, "So it's not that I'm lazy." I agreed that the list showed load, not lack of effort.

We agreed she would take the sheet home and talk to her parents about which batch helped least. I will meet her next week, and I have asked for a meeting with her parents too.

qa.q: How many hours did Hansa's week add up to?
How did Hansa feel before the meeting?
qa.a: Hansa felt inadequate and upset, believing she was not working hard enough, and had cried after a test.

qa.q: What else could the counsellor do to support Hansa?
qa.a: The counsellor could help Hansa build a simple weekly plan with rest blocks once a batch is dropped, and check how it feels next week.

qa.q: How might Lalremsiami see Hansa's discovery?
qa.a: Lalremsiami would likely feel relieved and glad she brought Hansa, seeing her friend stop blaming herself.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a Class 11 student adding up school, coaching, travel and homework, finding 62 hours with no rest and seeing the problem is load, not effort.
